cases.label: initial password of 41 characters ending in a space: SQL Server truncates the nvarchar(40) parameter, PostgreSQL's text parameter keeps the space
cases.reasoning: A string longer than a procedure parameter's declared length is silently truncated by SQL Server, so HASHBYTES hashes 40 'p' + FullName. The conversion declares initial_password as text, so it hashes 40 'p' + ' ' + FullName and the stored hash differs.

cases.label: initial password of 21 emoji (42 UTF-16 code units): SQL Server keeps 20 of them, PostgreSQL hashes all 21
cases.reasoning: nvarchar(40) counts UTF-16 code units; each emoji is a surrogate pair, so the parameter keeps 20 emoji. PostgreSQL's text keeps 21, and tsql_compat.utf16le encodes all of them, so the hash differs.

cases.label: password of 20 emoji (exactly 40 UTF-16 code units) and a full name with an emoji and a combining accent: surrogate pairs hashed as UTF-16LE
cases.reasoning: No truncation here: 20 emoji fill nvarchar(40) exactly. HASHBYTES hashes the UTF-16LE bytes including surrogate pairs; utf16le() must build the same pairs for code points above U+FFFF and leave 'e' + U+0301 unnormalised. A UTF-8 hash would differ.

cases.label: logon name of 51 characters: SQL Server truncates the nvarchar(50) parameter and completes; PostgreSQL's varchar(50) column rejects the value
cases.reasoning: SQL Server stores the first 50 characters in LogonName and the call completes. The conversion passes text into a varchar(50) column; PostgreSQL raises string_data_right_truncation (22001) because the extra character is not a space.

cases.label: logon name of 50 characters followed by three spaces: both engines store the 50 characters
cases.reasoning: SQL Server truncates the parameter to 50. PostgreSQL truncates a value for varchar(50) silently when the excess characters are all spaces, so both store the same 50 characters. The password 'pw ' keeps its own trailing space in the hash on both.

cases.label: NULL password and '' logon name; person 1's preferences are ''; the target's own preferences are replaced
cases.reasoning: NULL + FullName is NULL in T-SQL, so HASHBYTES returns NULL and HashedPassword becomes NULL; || and the STRICT utf16le() give NULL too. LogonName '' is stored as '' (not NULL). UserPreferences becomes person 1's '' even though person 2 had 'old'.

null-vs-empty.detail: empty string: yes; NULL in a text input: yes

cases.label: '' password and '' full name: SHA2_256 of zero bytes; LogonName NULL before
cases.reasoning: '' + '' is '' (not NULL), and HASHBYTES of an empty nvarchar is the SHA-256 of zero bytes. utf16le('') must return an empty bytea, not NULL, so sha256 gives the same digest.

null-vs-empty.detail: empty string: yes; NULL in a text input: yes

cases.label: full name and password differ only in case; the logon name keeps its case; two people share a full name
cases.reasoning: HASHBYTES is binary: 'AMY TREFL' + 'amy trefl' hashes differently from any case-folded form. Person 3 has the same FullName as person 2 and must stay untouched. LogonName 'Amy@Example.COM' is stored as given.

collation-case.detail: "amy trefl" and "AMY TREFL" differ only in case

top-ties.detail: two rows of Application.People share FullName = "amy trefl"

cases.label: person ids at the int limits and with gaps: activate 2147483647 while -2147483648 and 0 exist
cases.reasoning: PersonID is compared as int; the target sits at the int maximum and the other rows (0, -2147483648) must not change.

cases.label: NULL person id: nothing is updated and both engines raise
cases.reasoning: PersonID = NULL is never true, so @@ROWCOUNT is 0 and THROW 51000 runs; the conversion's NOT FOUND path raises P0001. No row changes.

cases.label: person 1 not yet enabled, called directly: refused, and its own row is unchanged
cases.reasoning: PersonID <> 1 excludes the template even when IsPermittedToLogon is 0, so the call raises and person 1 keeps its NULL logon and hash.

cases.label: an already-enabled person with an existing hash is refused and keeps the hash
cases.reasoning: IsPermittedToLogon = 0 is required. Person 2 is enabled with HashedPassword 0x00FF10; the call raises and the hash, logon name and preferences stay as they were.

objections.text: The hand-derived 'person 1 is refused' fixed case already calls the procedure for PersonID 1 while that person is not permitted to log on and requires the error path with unchanged table state. A11 changes only the logon name and template preferences, which the refused call does not read or write.

The hand-derived 'an already-enabled person is refused' fixed case already calls PersonID 2 with IsPermittedToLogon true and requires the error path with every Application.People value unchanged. Adding pre-existing logon, hash and preference values does not attack a different predicate or update mechanism.
